day_context.tournament_summary: There is no bigger fixture the game can hand you, and it has been twenty-four years since the World Cup last did. England and Argentina have not met at this tournament since 2002 — since David Beckham's penalty in Sapporo settled a private four-year debt — and now they are drawn together in a semi-final, in Atlanta, one win from the final. Everything about the pairing is loaded. There is 1966, when England beat Argentina at Wembley and their manager called the losing side 'animals.' There is 1986, four years after the Falklands War, when Diego Maradona beat England twice in four minutes — once with his hand, once with the greatest goal ever scored — and later called it revenge. There is 1998, the Beckham red card and the shootout that broke England. And there is tonight, the defending world champions against the country that has waited sixty years to reach another final. They meet again with the oldest grievance in the sport between them and a place at MetLife on the far side of it.
context_notes: England vs Argentina at Mercedes-Benz Stadium, Atlanta — the second World Cup semi-final; the winner reaches the July 19 final at MetLife.

It is the two nations' first World Cup meeting since 2002, and their sixth overall; the rivalry runs through 1966 (Rattín's sending-off and Alf Ramsey's 'animals'), 1986 (Maradona's 'Hand of God' and 'Goal of the Century', four years after the Falklands War) and the 1998 penalty shootout.
Argentina are the defending world champions, having won the 2022 final against France on penalties; a title here would be the first back-to-back World Cup since Brazil in 1958 and 1962.
England have not reached a World Cup final since they won the tournament in 1966 — a 60-year wait — though they reached the semi-finals in 1990 and 2018.
England reached this semi-final by beating Norway 2-1 after extra time in the quarter-final — settling, at last and when it counted, the ghost of Norway's famous 1981 win over them.

Argentina have ground their way here the hard way, needing extra time in both the Round of 32 (3-2 Cape Verde) and the quarter-final (3-1 Switzerland), with a 3-2 win over Egypt in the Round of 16 in between.

here_there_thread.framing: No two countries carry a heavier football grudge, and almost all of it was made at World Cups. It started at Wembley in 1966, when England beat Argentina 1-0 in a quarter-final so ill-tempered that the Argentine captain, Antonio Rattín, was sent off and refused to leave, and the England manager Alf Ramsey afterwards called the opposition 'animals' and stopped his players swapping shirts. It detonated in 1986, at the Estadio Azteca, four years after British and Argentine soldiers had killed each other over the Falkland Islands: Diego Maradona punched the ball past Peter Shilton, called it 'the Hand of God,' and four minutes later ran through half the England team to score what a global vote later named the greatest goal in World Cup history. He said, decades on, that it had felt like revenge for the war. Then 1998 — Michael Owen's wonder goal, David Beckham sent off for a flick of the boot at Diego Simeone, England out on penalties, Beckham burned in effigy back home. Then 2002, Beckham's penalty in Sapporo, the debt repaid. They have not met at a World Cup since. Twenty-four years later the draw has put them in a semi-final, and every one of those nights is in the room.

facts.label: Wembley, 1966
facts.fact: England beat Argentina 1-0 in the quarter-final; captain Antonio Rattín was sent off and refused to go, and Alf Ramsey called Argentina 'animals' — the incident helped inspire the invention of red and yellow cards.

facts.label: Azteca, 1986
facts.fact: Argentina beat England 2-1 in the quarter-final, four years after the Falklands War; Maradona scored the 'Hand of God' handball (51') and, four minutes later, the 'Goal of the Century' (55'), and later called the win a symbolic revenge for the war.

facts.label: Saint-Étienne, 1998
facts.fact: Argentina and England drew 2-2 — Owen's solo goal, Beckham sent off for kicking Simeone — and Argentina won the shootout 4-3, Paul Ince and David Batty missing.

facts.label: Sapporo, 2002
facts.fact: England beat Argentina 1-0 in the group stage, David Beckham scoring the winning penalty — his redemption four years after the red card — and it is the last time the two met at a World Cup, until tonight.

story_behind_number.surface_stat: England in a World Cup semi-final, and the number is 60
story_behind_number.historical_anchor: Sixty years ago, in 1966, England won the World Cup — the only time they have ever reached the final, let alone lifted it — and the tournament they won ran straight through Argentina, beaten 1-0 in a bad-tempered Wembley quarter-final on the way. Every England side since has chased that summer and failed to reach even the last game: the near-misses of Italia '90 and Russia 2018 got as far as the semi-final and no further, the penalty heartbreaks of the Euros stopped one round or one kick short. When the anthem 'Three Lions' promised, in 1996, that football was coming home after 'thirty years of hurt,' it was counting from 1966. That number is now sixty. Tonight England stand ninety minutes — against, of all opponents, Argentina — from the first World Cup final they will have contested since the day they won it. The wait is the story, and the team blocking it is the one they beat to start the clock.

supporting_context: England have not reached a World Cup final since winning the 1966 tournament on home soil; their deepest runs since were semi-final defeats in 1990 (to West Germany on penalties) and 2018 (to Croatia).
The 1966 World Cup, England's only final, included a 1-0 quarter-final win over Argentina — making tonight's opponent the team England beat en route to the very trophy they have chased ever since.
Argentina, by contrast, arrive as reigning champions seeking back-to-back titles; the asymmetry — one side ending a 60-year wait, the other defending the crown — is the whole shape of the night.

narrative_beats: It is the most famous quarter-final ever played, and it was never only about football. On 22 June 1986, at the Estadio Azteca, England met Argentina four years after the two countries had fought the Falklands War — a fact nobody in either camp pretended not to feel.

Six minutes into the second half, Diego Maradona rose with Peter Shilton and punched the ball into the net. The referee gave it. Maradona would call it 'a little of the hand of God' — the Hand of God — a goal that should not have counted and has never stopped being argued about.

Four minutes later he settled the argument another way. Collecting the ball inside his own half, he beat Beardsley, Reid, Butcher, Fenwick and then Shilton, and rolled it in: sixty yards, eleven touches, five England players, later voted in a global FIFA poll the greatest goal in World Cup history. Two goals, four minutes, one with his fist and one with everything he had.

Gary Lineker headed one back on 81 minutes and nearly forced a second, but Argentina held on 2-1, went on to beat West Germany in the final at the same stadium, and Maradona carried a nation. Years later he said the win over England had felt like revenge — 'we knew they had killed a lot of Argentine boys there... this was revenge.' The match has been shorthand for the whole rivalry ever since.

back_story.ledger: England and Argentina have met five times at a World Cup, and England actually lead it — three wins (1962, 1966, 2002), one loss (1986) and one draw (1998, which Argentina won on penalties). But the two defeats are the ones that echo: Maradona's Hand of God and Goal of the Century in 1986, four years after the Falklands War, and the 1998 shootout that sent David Beckham home a villain. England's wins were cleaner and quieter — a 3-1 in 1962, the 1-0 at Wembley in 1966 on the way to the title, Beckham's redemption penalty in 2002 — and they are the ones nobody outside England remembers. Tonight is the sixth meeting, the first since 2002, and the first ever with a World Cup final at stake.

video.title: Maradona's famous 8 minutes — Argentina 2-1 England, 1986
video.caption: The quarter-final that became shorthand for the whole rivalry: Argentina 2-1 England at the Estadio Azteca, 1986. In the space of four minutes Diego Maradona scored the 'Hand of God' with his fist and then the 'Goal of the Century' with a run past five England players — the two goals, one infamous and one immortal, that knocked England out four years after the Falklands War.

from_the_stands.question: Every time we play Argentina it feels like we lose — Maradona's hand, Beckham getting sent off, the shootout. Have we ever actually beaten them at a World Cup, or do I just remember the disasters?

facts: England actually lead the World Cup head-to-head with Argentina: five meetings, three England wins (1962, 1966, 2002), one loss (1986) and one draw (1998, which Argentina won on penalties).

England beat Argentina 3-1 in the 1962 group stage, 1-0 in the 1966 quarter-final at Wembley on the way to winning the tournament, and 1-0 again in the 2002 group stage through David Beckham's penalty.
The two defeats are the famous ones: the 1986 quarter-final (Maradona's Hand of God and Goal of the Century) and the 1998 Round of 16, drawn 2-2 with Beckham sent off, lost 4-3 on penalties.
Tonight is the sixth World Cup meeting and the first since 2002 — and the first with a place in the final on the line.
factual_brief.note: You remember the disasters because they were spectacular and they hurt — a handball that stood, the greatest goal ever scored, a red card and a shootout. But the record is the other way around: England have beaten Argentina at three World Cups and lost at only one, with the 1998 tie decided on penalties. The rivalry feels like a losing streak because the losses were unforgettable and the wins were ordinary. What's never happened, in any of the five, is the two of them meeting this late with this much at stake. Whatever tonight becomes, it won't be ordinary.

anomalies.tag: The oldest grudge, first final at stake
anomalies.seed: England and Argentina have met five times at a World Cup across sixty years of grievance — 1966, 1986, 1998 and more — but never once with a place in the final on the line, until tonight.

In the 1986 quarter-final Diego Maradona scored twice in four minutes against England — the 'Hand of God' handball and then the 'Goal of the Century' — the only time one player has produced football's most infamous goal and its most celebrated one in the same match.

England have not reached a World Cup final since they won the tournament in 1966 — a 60-year wait — and the team standing between them and one is Argentina, the same side they beat in the 1966 quarter-final on the way to the trophy.

Argentina arrive as reigning champions chasing the first back-to-back World Cup since Brazil in 1962, but they have needed extra time to survive both the Round of 32 and the quarter-final — grinding, not gliding, to the semi.
